subject: economics
title: Monopoly Power and Failure
welcome_lead: Even profitable monopolies can fail consumers and society.
meta_desc: A-Level Market Failure: monopoly power and information gaps.
final_note: Monopoly is efficient for the firm and inefficient for society.

concepts.def: Quantity consumers will buy at each price; falls as price rises.
Quantity producers will sell at each price; rises as price rises.
Where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Responsiveness of quantity to a price change.
Costs or benefits affecting third parties.

walkthroughs.body_html: The profit-maximising monopolist sets MR = MC. Price exceeds marginal cost - allocative inefficiency. Without rivalry, costs drift up - X-inefficiency.
Some industries - water pipes, rail tracks - have huge fixed costs and tiny marginal costs. One firm is cheapest, but must be regulated to prevent abuse.
Even a monopolist behaves competitively if entry is easy. Contestability matters more than the current number of firms. Lower sunk costs raise contestability.

mcqs.q: Are monopolies always bad for consumers?
options: Standard theory says monopolies restrict output and raise prices, but possible benefits include economies of scale, R&D investment and dynamic efficiency.
Monopolies are illegal and always harmful.

mcqs.q: What is asymmetric information as a source of market failure?
options: When one party in a transaction knows more than the other — leading to problems like adverse selection (used-car market) or moral hazard (insurance). Markets can fail or unravel when information is unequal.
Asymmetric information means a buyer and seller disagree about a price.
A negative externality is a tax on a business.
Asymmetric information is when a market only operates in one direction.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Moral hazard”?
options: Akerlof (1970) Market for Lemons: used car buyers know less than sellers, causing market unravelling.
Goods with positive externalities under-consumed by free market; e.g. vaccines, education.
Free market produces an allocation that is not Pareto efficient; sources include externalities, public goods, information failure.
Insured parties take more risk because they don't bear full costs; explains 2008 banking crisis behaviour.
